Messages.Author: Dr. Mosh
Messages.Body:

Aside from the fact that *anyone* can try it (you don't have to
be a rocket scientist to use Magic cards as marked ones), I don't dispute
this. I've said it before here on the newsgroups. The game is still
playable. Magic was, and Jyhad/V:tES will be.
It's not just about whether the game is playable or not. It's
about changing the dynamic of the game, adding a new (undesired) factor
to the game, and it's also about a lack of respect.
By adding mixed decks to the game, a certain element of the game
changes. Now some people will have marked decks not by choice, but by
force (best example: expansions. In every Magic expansion, there has
been at least one card that I decide is invaluable, and add to many of
my decks. This will happen in V:tES, and I will then have (for example)
only Necromancy cards with the Vampire backs and only vampires with
Necromancy with the Vampire backs). And others will have a very easy
time marking decks (a strategy which can be effective despite claims
that it doesn't "break the game").
Finally, the last thing, and perhaps the straw that pushes me
away from the game is the lack of respect implied in the change. I read
an interview with Dr. Garfield in which he stated that in playtesting
they found that AK cards with different backs didn't make a difference,
yet player preference was to keep the backs the same, and lo, the backs
were the same. Yet in Jyhad, even though marking decks is slightly
*more* advantageous (an assertation that I will defend, should anyone
want me to, in e-mail), the backs were changed anyway. This is not the
first time that Jyhad players have felt less respected than Magic
players, and by departing so drastically from the opinions we've
expressed, we feel that WotC does not care if we buy their game. I have
put forth the notion on several occassions that Magic is an A-title game
while Jyhad is a B-title. I still feel that way, and the name change is
just a confirmation in my mind of this trend. I don't have a problem
with this, but as someone who feels sleighted by this decision, I do not
see the need to purchase more of a game in which I have already
completed my investment, nor do I wish to "try" a game in which marking
will be a factor, because I don't have to be told how it will affect the
game, I know. It won't break the game, but it is still an effect that I
do not want. If WotC doesn't respect that opinion enough to abide by
it, I do not as a customer see a need to continue buying the game.

Messages.Author: Frank Alejano

: Agree. For another example, some openings in chess are so common that

: most masters have them memorized ahead for scores of moves in dozens of
: permutations. But are these openings restricted? ("Sorry Mr. Kasparov,
: you can only use one opening with the King's pawn.")

Not a valid association. The point that we are arguing over is not how
we play the game, it's what pieces we use to play the game. In that sense,
chess has ZERO variety, and for good reason- what would happen if I decided
to play with 1 King and 15 queens? Why on earth would I ever want to
play with a pawn (don't starts roasting me on chess tactics- you guys know
what I mean). WotC is trying to make a game much like chess, in that
a variety of tactics are viable, without one being dominant. Yes, taking
out multilands reduces the flexibilty of a deck. My Type I deck is
currently four colors, and I would not be able to do such a deck under
4e, but looking at my deck, one would notice that I have two main colors,
with white and black thrown in for their staple spells and nothing more
(Disenchant, Swords/Plows, Serras, Mind Twist, Tutor, Underworld Dreams).
What happens when I take out these two colors? I have to make up for gaping
holes in my deck with inferior versions of those spells. But that's what
I get for playing Red/Blue. There are very few strategies that require
three or more colors. The extra colors are usually thrown in for these
same reasons.

Yes, WotC is trying to dictate the play of the game, but not in a way
that would actually harm the game- they are trying to promote strategy,
both in deck building and playing. Choosing colors is supposed to be
a big part of the game, but never was with duals around. Now we're just
going to have to think a little more when building a deck.

Frank

As far as I'm concerned, Wizards of the Coast hasn't done anything to
destroy the enjoyment of Magic:The Gathering for people who play it for

fun. Tournaments can't possibly account for more than .01% of the games
of Magic played, at best, so changes in the rules for tourneys will have
relatively little impact overall on the game. People are free to play it
however they please, tourney legal or not, so unless major overhauls are
conducted in the actual core rules, WotC seems to be doing ok. The

'Demonic' cards deal was stupid, IMHO, but after seeing the ridiculous
levels to which people in the US seem to go to get things they don't like
banned, I can't say I'm surprised by it (still not happy, and I can't
agree with it, but at least I can now understand the rationale).

What is the big fuss over tournaments? Type I tournaments are still held
and can still be sanctioned. The store I represent is holding a Type I
(unsanctioned) tournament next month, and will be holding a Type II later
in the summer as well. Type II is certainly geared more towards allowing
the newer players to compete, and the only absence of fun I can see in
that respect is the sick thrill some people get out of trashing people
who have no chance. While I certainly think the rules could be altered or

improved upon, I hardly think that WotC is blindly adhering to a policy
geared towards removing all enjoyment from the game. Personally, I think

the number of expansions allowed in Type II should be from the Dark
on...it seems that WotC finally has a firm grasp on what constitutes a
too powerful card or expansion...and if one or two spoilers come up,
there is nothing preventing them from banning those cards from play or
restricting them. One card from the Dark (Maze of Ith) and none from
Fallen Empires doesn't seem like a bad thing to me.

Of course, there is always the issue of people not being able to play
with cards they may spent a great deal to aquire. Personally, I can't say
anything to this beyond,"Bad break, but what of it?". Type I tourneys
still exist, and there is nothing preventing you from using these cards
in casual play. If you're going to spend hundreds of dollars so you can
be competitive in a tournament, I can say only this- It's your choice.
There are thousands of Magic players out there who just want to play in a
tournament and have a chance, and that's what Type II seems geared
towards (although I agree it has its flaws). I lost a lot of sympathy for
some of the so called 'experienced' players when I saw their behaviour at
a recent trading night at a competitors store (note I'm just as
experienced as these people are...I've been playing Magic since
Alpha...matter of fact, I cracked open one of the first starter decks
that arrived in Winnipeg). These 'experienced' players were taking
advantage of kids who had started playing with revised. I saw people
trying to get dozens of multilands off of teens unaware that they had
been removed from 4th Edition, and not informing these kids that
multilands were discontinued. They were not amused with me when I
informed these kids that multilands were no longer in print. If this is
how the 'experienced' Type I supporters are going to behave...well, I am
certainly not going to take their side.

Just some random comments :)

Hmmm... this is a good point. However, I can think of two factors that
might influence WotC to make decisions in spite of customer response:

1) They think there are lots of unresponsive customers that they think
they'll lose if they follow the responsive (usually read, on the net at
least, as "a little obsessed with the game") customers' output.

2) They -- to put it bluntly --don't trust us (old customers) to know
what we like. They think that, if they leave multis in, we'll just
keep playing tons of Bolt-countermagic-Disenchant decks, and we'll get
bored and leave because the spoilers make the game too easy. They
have acknowledged that overpowered building blocks have to exist,
and that they don't want to see lots of said blocks in decks.

I don't quite understand how they could think this myself, but I want to
make clear a point that has been implied in a number of threads -- tourney
rules do *partially* determine what goes into decks, but, in fun play,
most of what determines deck content is your play group. If I say
"I wanna play my spoiler-laden white everything denial deck," then someone
will respond "okay, I'll test my equally spoiler-laden vice mine deck
against it," or he/she'll say "put that damn thing away before we hurt
you." Fun play rapidly evolves once people get bored with mass death.
Remember the initial evolution of Magic? I think it was Garfield himself
(or maybe Zak Dolan) who said it: the game went from "can I win?" -- which
anyone with tons of money and a modicum of experience can do -- to "can I
win with this deck, or something like it?" Fun groups will sneer at stupid
boring killer decks. Now, playing 16 artifacts in one turn and sacrificing
*all* of them, now *that's* cool.

Dave G.

Great. So follow your own vision, and play with all of the cards that

reason you *have* to do that unless you're playing in a tournament, or testing

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie

Charles M. Kozierok <i...@rice-chex.ai.mit.edu> wrote:

>I cannot believe that WotC is acting so dense about this particular

>issue. It is really very simple: the rules of the game, as laid
>out in the starter-deck rulebooks, do not work. They lead to
>degenerate decks and boring games. So people *have to* find an
>alternative. Of the three choices (start deck rules, arbitrary local
>rules, and tournament rules), tournament rules are the least problematic.

That is not necessarily true. What is best for tournaments is not necessarily
best for private play. Simple example: Shahrazad. This is only banned
because it makes matches take forever, which is not necessarily a concern
in private play.

Tournament play and private play are not synonymous. Most games exist
perfectly well with tournament rules that are ignored in private play.
The whole point to having *tournament* rules is that they are a construct
which is added on to the basic game, not something that is required for
the game to be viable.

In the ideal trading card game, there should be no reason to have to tell
people not to play with their cards, except for certain special cases like
ante. When you think about it, even putting a four card limit on all cards
is telling people not to play with their fifth, sixth, etc card. Restricting
a card is even worse... not only do repetitions of a card become worthless
that much quicker, it becomes that much harder to trade away the excess.

The deck construction rules for Magic are only necessary in any sense once
you get into wild, trading environments where people are buying cards by
the boxful, not a couple of boosters at the time. While this is unfortunate,
it's not terribly surprising given that no one was expecting people to
routinely spend hundreds of dollars buying Magic cards. But the best solution
to the situation is not to saddle the game with deck construction rules.
The best solution is to balance the card set to the point where deck
construction rules are not necessary at all, and leave those rules for
tournament environments where people are playing with the older, broken cards.

legal. What, you think everybody who builds their decks to Type I or
Type II standards is testing out a tournament deck? No, they're being
good folks, and not building degenerate decks! WITHOUT DECK
CONSTRUCTION GUIDELINES, MAGIC IS NOT A VIABLE GAME. The broken cards
in a no-guideline-game are on the COMMON sheet! Nobody'd bother with
Forks, Balances, Shaharazads, Time Elementals, etc... They'd be
useless. It'd be a matter of who could go first, basically. Deck
construction guidelines are an absolute necessity for the survival of
the game. Once upon a time, WotC recognized this. I think they may have
forgotten. Go ahead, run a no-limits 4E *ONLY* game. Then go back
and decide carefully what sort of limits you want to continue to impose.
Maybe you'll understand why people will go, "You're not playing a tournament
legal deck? I won't play you." Because once it's known that it's not
tournament legal, it opens up the host of degeneracies that are available.
*THAT* is why WotC *MUST* give some deck construction guidelines, other
than 40 cards minimum, period.

I understand that it's not something that WotC thinks should be
necessary, but even without the horribly broken 3 for 1 cards (that's
Lightning Bolt, Healing Salve, Dark Ritual, Giant Growth, Ancestral Recall)
the decks can STILL be far too powerful without limits. That means that
some limits will HAVE be used.

The problem then becomes what deck construction rules to use.
Well, there is one set, and ONLY one set of rules which are known to
every player of the game. (Barring the set in the IBR, which is effectively
no rules...) That set is the tournament rules.

Frankly, I think that a deck of just 32 llanawar elves and 9 basic
forests is even scarier than the lightning bolt deck... *grin* The
basic idea here is that the deck construction rules in the Itty-Bitty
(not so itty-bitty anymore) rulebook are *BROKEN*. The cards that
make it so, are not on the rare sheet, either. They're on the common
sheet. For $3, I could build a terrifyingly successful, but annoying
deck.

>In the ideal trading card game, there should be no reason to have to tell
>people not to play with their cards, except for certain special cases like
>ante. When you think about it, even putting a four card limit on all cards
>is telling people not to play with their fifth, sixth, etc card. Restricting
>a card is even worse... not only do repetitions of a card become worthless
>that much quicker, it becomes that much harder to trade away the excess.

Well, it encourages them to play with more than one deck, if you
limit it to four and they have more than four. Four's a good number
though, and I think it's been too long since you've been bored to
tears by a LB/Mountain deck. If you saw one again today, you'd
remember, I think, why deck construction rules exist.

>The deck construction rules for Magic are only necessary in any sense once
>you get into wild, trading environments where people are buying cards by
>the boxful, not a couple of boosters at the time. While this is unfortunate,

Tom, once and for all, it's not the restricted list or the banned
list that I (and many others) care about. It's deck construction
rules that are friendly to everyone, available to everyone, and
supported by WotC. That's all I'm looking for. Frankly, being
familiar as I am with the politics of fandom, I don't believe in the
long run of a Players Convocation. You've got folks paid to do that.
The players won't, they don't have time, or money, to do that. All we
need is an article in the Duelist, outlining a few individually named
'styles' of deck construction. A restricted list that includes the
banned-for-tournament-play cards, for example. Maybe some good
suggestions for setting up bubble-leagues in the area. (We've got a
few really GOOD bubble leagues in this area, which folks are excited
about...) That sort of thing would revolutionize interest in ante games,
in fun-play, basically making the tournament types NOT THE ONLY TYPE THAT
EVERYBODY RECOGNIZES.

Anything like that. I agree, I can come up with rules to play by,
local rules, I can meet damned near any construction guideline
challenge. *BUT* I need to be able to express to someone else in
simple terms what guidelines my deck is constructed under. And the
only way to do that in a *REAL* way, so that I can go to Scotland and
they'll understand, so I can go to New York, and they'll understand,
etc., is to have WotC present and support it. Not as a tournament
type necessarily, but as a supported guideline nonetheless.

The IBR's guidelines are broken, even in 4E only environments. I
believe you know that. I believe you'll (as WotC) fix it... I'd just
like to have some idea as to when, and maybe a LITTLE input on how.

There are certainly ways to balance a game without card limits without
making a Jyhad knockoff. INWO (revised), for example. Magic, however,
may not be able to do this without drastically overhauling the rules. The
apparent failure to avoid all card limits with Ice Ages does raise the
question of whether an unlimited Magic is possible, or at any rate
practical.

The alternative, however, is rather brutal. If Magic needs card limits,
the proliferation of new cards is almost guaranteed to eventually break
the game regardless of card limits. Over time, you will see cards with a
similar effect to Lightning Bolt (like Chain Lightning). When there are
10 of them, Bolt decks will work fine under 4-card.

If Wizards wants a long-term success in Magic, they must escape the
Millstone of card limits. The type II rules, incidentally, are one way to
fix the proliferation problem - ban ALL old cards and semi-broken cards
ban be managed with limits again. Of course, that tees off customers as
the cards have built-in obsolesence.
